notes:
CONFLICT WITH THE ESTABLISHMENT - STUDY NOTES

Note: this chapter is in Part 3 of the section, called ‘The Message in Conflict’. It is a short chapter. The topic is also looked at in Section H (The Bible: Literature and Sacred Text) and Section C (World Religions).

OPENING QUOTE (LUKE 14:2-4)
- ‘Just then in front of him, there was a man who had dropsy. And Jesus asked the lawyers and Pharisees, “Is it lawful to cure people on the sabbath, or not?” But they were silent.’
- This sets the theme: Jesus in conflict with those in power over the meaning of the Law.

KEY TERMS
- Treason: the crime of betraying or challenging the ruler or state. From the Roman point of view Jesus was charged with treason.
- Sabbath: the Jewish holy day of rest, when work was forbidden by the Law.
- Blasphemy: insulting God or claiming for yourself what belongs only to God. The scribes thought Jesus was guilty of blasphemy when he forgave sins.
- Passover: the Jewish feast for which Jesus and many pious Jews travelled to Jerusalem to worship at the Temple.
- Establishment: the people and groups in power - here the Roman authorities and the Jewish religious leaders.

TWO KINDS OF CONFLICT
- 1. Conflict with Roman imperial values (the Romans).
- 2. Conflict with the Jewish religious establishment (Pharisees, scribes, Sadducees, chief priests).

PART 1: JESUS’ CHALLENGE TO ROMAN IMPERIAL VALUES

WHY JESUS COULD NOT BE IGNORED
- Given the social and political situation of the time, it is not surprising that the message of this wandering teacher excited some people and upset many.
- Things that meant Jesus of Nazareth could not be ignored:
- the stories he told
- the people he associated with
- the places he visited
- the things he said directly to those in power.
- He came at a crucial moment in the history of Judaism.
- Jesus challenged those in power AND the nature of power itself.

JESUS RECALLS GOD’S MESSAGE
- Jesus reminded those who had forgotten of Yahweh’s message to the people:
- Yahweh was their God and they were the chosen people.
- They were called to love the Lord their God with all their hearts and to ‘love your neighbour as yourself’.
- Under Roman domination, this connectedness to their God was in danger of being lost.

THE KINGDOM OF GOD AS A CHALLENGE TO CAESAR
- Jesus proclaimed the Kingdom of God.
- The Romans could have seen this as challenging the rule of Caesar.
- The Kingdom of God could have been understood as a direct challenge to the power of Imperial Rome.

PILATE AND JESUS AT THE ‘TRIAL’ (JOHN 18)
- Pilate’s question was an attempt to justify the Roman position: ‘Are you the King of the Jews?’ (John 18:33)
- Jesus does not reply directly, but he talks about his kingdom: ‘My kingdom is not from this world. If my kingdom were from this world, my followers would be fighting to keep me from being handed over to the Jews.’ (John 18:36)
- Pilate replies: ‘So you are a king?’ (John 18:37) - and Jesus does not deny it.
- Jesus’ idea of kingship and the Kingdom of God was completely different from that of Pilate and the Roman authorities.
- But his admission gave them the excuse to sentence him to death.

THE CLAIM TO BE MESSIAH (LUKE 23:2)
- Jesus’ claim to be the Messiah or ‘Anointed One’ was further evidence of the threat he posed to Rome.
- His Jewish enemies were quick to point this out: ‘We found this man perverting our nation, forbidding us to pay taxes to the emperor, and saying that he himself is the Messiah, a king.’ (Luke 23:2)
- Three accusations in Luke 23:2: perverting the nation; forbidding taxes to the emperor; claiming to be Messiah, a king.
- But (as seen in chapter 6) Jesus’ idea of himself as Messiah did not match any Jewish expectation of the time.
- He certainly did not pose a military or political threat to the Roman Empire.

THE REAL THREAT: A NEW SET OF VALUES
- Pilate and others may have realised in some way the very real threat that Jesus’ life and message posed to the value systems of the time.
- In God’s kingdom everything would be different:
- the first would be last and the last first
- the poor would be blessed
- those who suffered would rejoice.
- The Kingdom of God would mean radical changes for those who embraced it.
- God would be present to all people, and care for others would be the sign of this presence.
- There is no doubt Jesus knew he was in danger because of the message he preached and lived.
- From the Roman point of view he was charged with TREASON and condemned to death by CRUCIFIXION.

PART 2: JESUS IN CONFLICT WITH THE JEWISH RELIGIOUS ESTABLISHMENT

SPIRIT OF THE LAW VERSUS LETTER OF THE LAW
- Jesus came into conflict with the Pharisees more than once.
- His vision of the renewal and restoration of the Kingdom of God threatened the Jewish religious establishment.
- Jesus interpreted the SPIRIT of the Law. The Pharisees had a very LITERAL interpretation of the Law. These often clashed.
- Jesus preached love of God and love of neighbour over a literal reading of the Law.
- The rule against work on the Sabbath was to be ignored if someone needed help.
- Jesus criticised the hypocrisy of those who kept the letter of the Law but showed no compassion for those considered unworthy.

STORY 1: HEALING THE MAN WITH DROPSY ON THE SABBATH (LUKE 14:1-6)
- Took place in the home of a leader of the Pharisees.
- Jesus challenged the Pharisees on their literal reading of the Law.
- He asked: ‘Is it lawful to cure people on the sabbath, or not?’ The Pharisees could not answer.
- He asked again: ‘If one of you has a child or an ox that has fallen into a well, will you not immediately pull it out on a sabbath day?’
- They could not reply to this.
- Point: helping someone in need matters more than the rule against Sabbath work.

STORY 2: THE PARALYSED MAN LET DOWN THROUGH THE ROOF (MARK’S GOSPEL)
- Because of the crowds around the house, a paralysed man had to be let down through the roof to reach Jesus.
- Jesus’ first words to him: ‘Son, your sins are forgiven.’
- This angered the scribes present, because they said only God could forgive sin.
- In their eyes, Jesus had committed BLASPHEMY - a very serious charge.
- Jesus then cured the man to show the authority of the Son of Man on earth.
- The scribes became even more indignant.

STORY 3: THE CLEANSING OF THE TEMPLE (MARK 11:15-18)
- Jesus travelled to Jerusalem during the feast of PASSOVER, like many pious Jews, to worship at the Temple.
- The city would have been very busy with large crowds of worshippers.
- The gospels show many signs that Jesus was aware of the growing tension around him and his followers.
- In the Temple, Jesus:
- drove out those who were selling and buying
- overturned the tables of the money-changers
- overturned the seats of those who sold doves
- would not let anyone carry anything through the Temple.
- He taught: ‘Is it not written, “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations”? But you have made it a den of robbers.’
- When the chief priests and scribes heard it, they kept looking for a way to kill him.
- They were afraid of him, because the whole crowd was spellbound by his teaching.

RESULT OF THE CONFLICT
- These words and actions were a direct challenge to:
- the institution of the Temple
- the authority of the Pharisees and the Sadducees.
- All these actions threatened the Jewish religious establishment.
- They were now actively seeking to charge Jesus and have him arrested.
- The charge and the reasons behind it are looked at in the next chapter (The Death and Resurrection of Jesus).

DISCUSSION STORY: JOHN AND JOE
- John (40) is a wonderful father and faithful husband, works hard, goes to church every Sunday with his children, keeps the commandments, and visits the sick and elderly.
- Joe (40) has been an alcoholic since his teens, beats his wife in drunken rages (neighbours give her refuge), sometimes drinks all his dole money so his children go hungry or depend on the Vincent de Paul. His children are terrified and receiving counselling. He hasn’t been to church for years.
- Both die. Joe is taken into heaven before John and given a higher place in the Kingdom of God.
- Question: What is your reaction? (Links to ‘the first will be last and the last first’ and why Jesus’ message upset people.)

FOR REFLECTION: ‘ONE SOLITARY LIFE’
- A reflection on Jesus’ life: born in an obscure village, child of a peasant woman; worked in a carpenter shop until thirty; then three years as an itinerant (travelling) preacher.
- He never owned a home, wrote a book, held an office, had a family, went to college, put his foot inside a big city, or travelled two hundred miles from where he was born.
- ‘He had no credentials but himself.’
- Popular opinion turned against him; friends ran away; one denied him; he was handed to his enemies; went through the mockery of a trial; nailed to a cross between two thieves; executioners gambled for his coat; laid in a borrowed grave through the pity of a friend.
- ‘Nineteen long centuries’ later he is the centrepiece of the human race.
- All the armies, navies, parliaments and kings put together have not affected human life as powerfully as ‘that ONE SOLITARY LIFE’.
- Question: How do you explain the impact of the life of Jesus?

TEXTBOOK QUESTIONS AND ASSIGNMENTS
- What was the message of this wandering teacher that excited some and upset many?
- Why was Jesus condemned to death by Pontius Pilate?
- How did Jesus offend the Jewish religious leadership?
- Identify two key elements of Jesus’ vision and message seen as a threat to Roman imperial values.
- Identify two key elements of Jesus’ vision of renewal and restoration that threatened the Jewish religious establishment.

QUICK REVISION CHECKLIST
- Threat to Rome: Kingdom of God vs rule of Caesar; ‘King of the Jews’ (John 18:33-37); Messiah claim (Luke 23:2); new values (first last, poor blessed) -> treason -> crucifixion.
- Threat to Jewish leaders: spirit vs letter of Law; Sabbath healing of man with dropsy (Luke 14:1-6); forgiving sins of paralysed man = blasphemy (Mark); cleansing of the Temple at Passover (Mark 11:15-18) -> challenge to Temple, Pharisees and Sadducees.

rows.explanation: The chapter says Jesus challenged those in power and the nature of power itself.

rows.prompt: Which of these is NOT listed as a reason Jesus could not be ignored?
rows.explanation: The chapter lists his stories, the people he associated with, the places he visited and what he said to those in power.

As a challenge to the rule of Caesar

It made the crowds crown him
It gave the excuse to sentence him to death

rows.prompt: In Luke 23:2, Jesus’ enemies accused him of forbidding what?

It meant he would leave Palestine
It meant he was a Temple priest
It could be seen as a claim to be a king

The strong would rule the weak

rows.explanation: God would be present to all people and care for others would be the sign of this presence.

rows.explanation: From the Roman point of view he was charged with treason and condemned to death by crucifixion.

rows.explanation: Jesus’ interpretation of the spirit of the Law often conflicted with their very literal interpretation.

rows.explanation: He criticised the hypocrisy of those who upheld the letter of the Law but showed no compassion for the ‘unworthy’.

rows.prompt: What illness did the man healed on the Sabbath in Luke 14 have?
rows.explanation: In Luke 14:1-6 Jesus heals a man with dropsy on the Sabbath.

options: In the home of a leader of the Pharisees
At the house of Simon the leper

They had him arrested at once

He was carried into the Temple

They said the man was a Roman

rows.explanation: What Jesus had done amounted to blasphemy in their eyes - a very serious charge.

To prove he was a priest
To gain the support of Rome
To show the authority of the Son of Man on earth

rows.prompt: For which feast did Jesus travel to Jerusalem?
rows.explanation: Jesus travelled to Jerusalem during the feast of Passover, as did many pious Jews.

rows.explanation: He overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold doves (Mark 11:15).

rows.prompt: Complete the quote: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for…’
rows.explanation: Jesus said, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations’, but they had made it a den of robbers.

options: He had an army of followers
The whole crowd was spellbound by his teaching
He threatened to destroy the city
rows.explanation: Mark 11:18 says they were afraid because the whole crowd was spellbound by his teaching.

rows.prompt: Jesus’ actions in the Temple directly challenged the authority of which groups?
rows.explanation: The chapter says these actions challenged the Temple and the authority of the Pharisees and Sadducees.

rows.prompt: In ‘One Solitary Life’, until what age did Jesus work in a carpenter shop?
rows.explanation: The reflection says he worked in a carpenter shop until he was thirty, then preached for three years.

rows.prompt: Explain why the Romans may have seen the Kingdom of God as a threat.
rows.model_answer: Jesus proclaimed the Kingdom of God, which could be understood as a direct challenge to the rule of Caesar and the power of Imperial Rome. His claim to be Messiah was also presented as a claim to be a king (Luke 23:2). In God’s kingdom values would be turned upside down: the first last, the poor blessed.

rows.prompt: Describe the exchange between Pilate and Jesus in John 18:33-37.
rows.model_answer: Pilate asked, ‘Are you the King of the Jews?’ Jesus did not answer directly but said, ‘My kingdom is not from this world,’ or his followers would be fighting for him. Pilate said, ‘So you are a king?’ and Jesus did not deny it, which gave the excuse to sentence him to death.

rows.prompt: Name the three accusations made against Jesus in Luke 23:2.
rows.model_answer: His enemies said he was perverting the nation, forbidding people to pay taxes to the emperor, and saying that he himself was the Messiah, a king.

rows.prompt: Name three ways things would be different in God’s kingdom, according to the chapter.
rows.model_answer: The first would be last and the last first; the poor would be blessed; and those who suffered would rejoice. God would be present to all people, and care for others would be the sign of this presence.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between Jesus’ and the Pharisees’ interpretation of the Law.
rows.model_answer: The Pharisees interpreted the Law very literally. Jesus looked to the spirit of the Law, putting love of God and love of neighbour first, so that the rule against work on the Sabbath should be ignored if someone needed help. He criticised the hypocrisy of those who kept the letter of the Law but had no compassion.

rows.prompt: Describe the healing of the man with dropsy (Luke 14:1-6).
rows.model_answer: In the home of a leader of the Pharisees on the Sabbath, Jesus asked, ‘Is it lawful to cure people on the sabbath, or not?’ They were silent. He then asked whether they would not pull out a child or an ox that fell into a well on the Sabbath, and they could not reply.

rows.prompt: Why did the healing of the paralysed man anger the scribes?
rows.model_answer: Jesus first said to the man, ‘Son, your sins are forgiven.’ The scribes believed only God could forgive sin, so they saw this as blasphemy, a very serious charge. When Jesus then cured the man to show the authority of the Son of Man, they became even more indignant.

rows.prompt: Describe what Jesus did in the Temple in Mark 11:15-18.
rows.model_answer: At Passover Jesus drove out the buyers and sellers, overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold doves, and let no one carry anything through the Temple. He said, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations’, but they had made it ‘a den of robbers’. The chief priests and scribes then looked for a way to kill him.

rows.prompt: (a) Identify two key elements of Jesus’ message that were perceived as a threat to Roman imperial values. (b) Explain why Jesus was condemned to death by Pontius Pilate.
rows.model_answer:
(a) First, Jesus proclaimed the Kingdom of God. This could have been seen by the Romans as challenging the rule of Caesar and as a direct challenge to the power of Imperial Rome. Second, the values of the Kingdom turned the Roman world upside down: the first would be last and the last first, the poor would be blessed and those who suffered would rejoice. God would be present to all people and care for others would be the sign of this presence. Jesus challenged both those in power and the nature of power itself.
(b) At his ‘trial’ Pilate asked, ‘Are you the King of the Jews?’ (John 18:33). Jesus said, ‘My kingdom is not from this world’ (John 18:36), but when Pilate asked, ‘So you are a king?’ he did not deny it. His idea of kingship was completely different from Pilate’s, but his admission gave the excuse to sentence him. His Jewish enemies also accused him of perverting the nation, forbidding taxes to the emperor and claiming to be ‘the Messiah, a king’ (Luke 23:2). Although he was no military or political threat, from the Roman point of view he was charged with treason and condemned to death by crucifixion.
rows.marking_scheme: (a) 2 elements x 5 marks (identify 2 + explain 3). May refer to: Kingdom of God vs rule of Caesar; reversal of values (first last, poor blessed); challenge to power itself; Messiah/king claim. (b) 10 marks: very good 8-10, good 5-7, fair 0-4. May refer to: John 18:33-37; did not deny being king; Luke 23:2 accusations; treason; crucifixion; not a real military threat.

rows.prompt: Identify two key elements of Jesus’ vision of renewal and restoration that threatened the Jewish religious establishment. Refer to gospel stories in your answer.
rows.model_answer: One key element was Jesus’ interpretation of the spirit of the Law rather than its letter. The Pharisees had a very literal interpretation, but Jesus preached love of God and love of neighbour over this, so the rule against Sabbath work was to be ignored if someone needed help. In Luke 14:1-6, in the home of a leader of the Pharisees, he healed a man with dropsy and asked, ‘Is it lawful to cure people on the sabbath, or not?’ They were silent. He asked if they would not pull a child or an ox out of a well on the Sabbath, and they could not reply. He also criticised the hypocrisy of those with no compassion. A second element was Jesus’ claim to authority. In Mark’s gospel a paralysed man was let down through the roof, and Jesus said, ‘Son, your sins are forgiven.’ The scribes saw this as blasphemy, since only God could forgive sin. He then cured the man to show the authority of the Son of Man. Finally, at Passover he cleansed the Temple (Mark 11:15-18), overturning the tables of the money-changers and calling it ‘a den of robbers’. This directly challenged the Temple and the authority of the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the chief priests and scribes looked for a way to kill him.
rows.marking_scheme: 2 elements x 10 marks: identify 2 marks, explain with gospel evidence 8 marks. May refer to: spirit vs letter of the Law; Sabbath; man with dropsy Luke 14:1-6; hypocrisy and compassion; forgiving sins/blasphemy (paralysed man, Mark); cleansing of the Temple Mark 11:15-18; challenge to Temple, Pharisees, Sadducees.

rows.prompt: Describe the cleansing of the Temple and explain why it angered the religious leaders.
rows.model_answer: Jesus went to Jerusalem for the feast of Passover, when the city was crowded with worshippers. In Mark 11:15-18 he entered the Temple and drove out those buying and selling, overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves, and would not let anyone carry anything through the Temple. He taught, ‘Is it not written, “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations”? But you have made it a den of robbers.’ This angered the leaders because it was a direct challenge to the institution of the Temple and to the authority of the Pharisees and Sadducees. The chief priests and scribes kept looking for a way to kill him, because they were afraid of him: the whole crowd was spellbound by his teaching.
rows.marking_scheme: Description 5 marks (Passover, drove out sellers, tables of money-changers, seats of dove-sellers, ‘house of prayer’/‘den of robbers’). Explanation 5 marks (challenge to Temple institution and authority of Pharisees/Sadducees; crowd spellbound; leaders afraid and sought to kill him).

rows.prompt: Explain the meaning of blasphemy and show how this charge arose in Jesus’ ministry.
rows.model_answer: Blasphemy means insulting God or claiming for oneself what belongs to God alone. In the time of Jesus it was a very serious charge. In Mark’s gospel a paralysed man was let down through the roof of a house because of the crowds around Jesus. Jesus’ first words to him were, ‘Son, your sins are forgiven.’ The scribes who were present were angry, because they said only God could forgive sin, so in their eyes Jesus had committed blasphemy. Jesus then cured the man to show the authority of the Son of Man on earth, which made the scribes even more indignant. Along with his Sabbath healings and the cleansing of the Temple, this threatened the Jewish religious establishment, who began actively seeking to charge Jesus and have him arrested.
rows.marking_scheme: Meaning of blasphemy 3 marks. Story of paralysed man (roof, ‘your sins are forgiven’, scribes, only God forgives) 5 marks. Consequence (cure shows authority of Son of Man; leaders seek to charge him) 2 marks.
